classification.tone: Grounded, paranoid, escalating, with darkly comic FBI banter and a cosmic dread undercurrent

evaluation.positioning_hook: A rookie FBI agent chasing missing ex-cons in Silver Lake stumbles into a comet-fueled conspiracy, a hidden basement cult, and a bureau cover-up that turns her grief into a weapon.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean commercial engine: an FBI stakeout, a comet overhead, and a hidden conspiracy that keeps widening. The hook is accessible to thriller audiences, with enough genre escalation to travel beyond a niche sci-fi lane.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The script establishes its engine early: Rico and Cole surveil the wrong house, then discover a second house, a basement system, and a larger pattern tied to the comet. The premise is easy to explain in a sentence and the story keeps sharpening that sentence as it goes.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Rico has a strong internal engine through her mother’s disappearance, her need to be right, and her outsider status inside the bureau. Cole gives the story a lived-in partner dynamic, while Watson and James add distinct pressure points, though the character web is strongest around Rico rather than evenly distributed.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldest move is making surveillance procedure the doorway into cosmic horror and institutional conspiracy. The foil-lined basement, the sound-based creature logic, and the bureau’s bureaucratic use of the phenomenon give the material a confident, unusual identity.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps escalating through reversals: red door versus blue door, the hidden hatch, the support group connection, the reveal of Watson, and the final descent into the dungeon. Each turn adds a new layer of danger or meaning, and the ending lands with a full-feature payoff.

resonant_originality.reasoning: This feels like a conspiracy thriller that keeps revealing a stranger, more inevitable version of itself. The comet motif, the tinfoil acoustics, and the idea of a federal asset pipeline for the unexplained make the premise feel fresh rather than borrowed.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The FBI field office, the surveillance van, the Silver Lake neighborhood, the support group, and the hidden domestic bunker all carry specific texture. The world is story-generating, though the most vivid density lives in the central conspiracy rather than in a broad social ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very identifiable tonal blend: procedural banter, suburban absurdity, and creeping body-horror paranoia. The cup-o-noodles, tacos, dinner bell, and support-group scenes keep the material from sitting in one register.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the thriller mechanics is a grief story about memory, self-mythology, and the need to make chaos mean something. The final reveal that Rico’s childhood memory was altered gives the script a deeper psychological layer that re-frames the entire story.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Rico and Cole have a strong lead-partner dynamic, and Watson/James each create useful pressure, but the story still lives primarily through Rico’s point of view. The ensemble is functional and memorable, though not yet a true multi-directional engine.

casting_characteristics: One child version of Rico in flashback
Supporting roles with Latino identity in the FBI and ex-con world

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with recurring exterior street, yard, and hill coverage
notable_requirements: Contained residential neighborhood with two adjacent houses and a shared garage
FBI field office and surveillance van builds
Hospital, support group room, diner, motel, and city hall exteriors

technical.vfx_details: Comet Theora, atmospheric light effects, creature transformations, and final sky/lift imagery require visible but not tentpole-level VFX.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, injury makeup, foil-lined set dressing, creature prosthetics/appendages, and breakaway elements in the dungeon and roof sequence.

rights_flags.detail: Patriot Act, NSA, FBI, LAPD, Sinaloa Cartel, Best Buy, Reynolds Wrap, QuickTime Player, Bud Light, Taco Stand, and Cup-o-Noodles are all named on the page.
No real people are named, but the story references public institutions and a specific support-group setting.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming feature or premium-cable theatrical genre lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Best positioned as a festival-to-platform or streamer-original feature with genre-forward marketing.

cost.note: The story is largely contained to a few recurring spaces, but the comet effects, creature work, and dungeon finale push it above a microbudget lane.

cast.note: The lead roles are compact, but the project benefits from strong casting in Rico, Cole, Watson, and James, plus a child Rico flashback.

location.note: The core story is contained to a neighborhood and a handful of interiors, though the script still moves through multiple distinct spaces including flashbacks and institutional locations.

content.note: Violence, torture imagery, body horror, drugging, and a mature conspiracy framework narrow the content lane.

rights.note: The script uses several named brands and institutions, but no major life-rights or franchise IP dependency is present.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The surveillance setup is a story engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The FBI van, the bugs, the monitors, and the stakeout mechanics give the movie a built-in visual grammar and a clean commercial frame. Buyers who want a contained thriller with a distinctive procedural spine will see a producible hook that still feels cinematic.
strengths.evidence: Rico and Cole spend the first act building the surveillance operation, then the monitors become the audience’s window into the hidden house and the dungeon below.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Rico is built around grief and obsession.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead role has the kind of emotional contradiction that can anchor a genre movie and give an actor real range: competence, denial, guilt, and stubbornness. Prestige-minded buyers and actors looking for a showcase lead will respond to a protagonist whose casework is inseparable from her childhood wound.
strengths.evidence: Her mother’s disappearance, the recurring comet memory, and the way she keeps pushing the case even after Watson tells her to stand down.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tonal blend is unusually specific.
strengths.what_it_means: The script can play as a thriller, a horror piece, and a dark workplace comedy without losing its identity, which broadens its audience lane. Directors and buyers who like genre material with personality will respond to the cup-o-noodles, taco-run, and dinner-bell banter sitting beside the dread.
strengths.evidence: Cole’s eating habits, the FBI office banter, the taco stand stakeout, and the bell that quiets the room.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The hidden-house reveal is a strong midpoint engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The red-door/blue-door misdirection gives the movie a clean, memorable turn that reorients the entire investigation. That kind of reveal is valuable to producers because it creates a trailer moment and a structural pivot without requiring a huge scale jump.
strengths.evidence: The audience learns the suspect is next door, not in the house Rico has been bugging, and the wardrobe opens into the basement passage.

strengths.what_it_means: Watson’s use of the assets turns the story from a one-off monster hunt into a larger system with repeatable logic, which is exactly what makes a genre concept feel bigger than one case. Buyers who want franchise-adjacent mythology without IP baggage will see room here.
strengths.evidence: Watson explains the bureau has been managing the creatures as part of the counterterrorism apparatus and using them to generate intelligence.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The comet gives the movie a deadline and a mood.
strengths.what_it_means: The celestial clock adds urgency while also giving the film a visual signature that separates it from standard cop-thriller fare. Genre buyers and marketing teams can sell the sky as an active force, not just a backdrop.
strengths.evidence: Comet Theora is repeatedly tracked, discussed online, and ultimately becomes the event that coincides with the final confrontation.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending pays off the emotional premise.
strengths.what_it_means: The final reveal that Rico’s memory was altered and that the bureau has been shaping the narrative gives the movie a strong aftertaste and a rewatchable final turn. Festival audiences and streamer viewers both respond to a genre ending that recontextualizes the lead’s entire emotional journey.
strengths.evidence: The childhood flashback is revised, Watson reframes her mother’s disappearance, and Rico ends in a support-group-to-closure-to-conspiracy loop that lands on the final Bora Bora image.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, high-concept thriller with a real identity: FBI surveillance as the doorway into a comet-driven conspiracy, a hidden basement system, and a lead role powered by grief and obsession. It has the kind of procedural-to-horror escalation that producers can package, actors can sink into, and buyers can market with a single image: the wrong house, the right sky, and a bureau that’s been watching all along.

lead_characters.name: Lucia Del Rico
lead_characters.hook: Rico is a sharp, restless junior agent whose competence is always colliding with her need to prove something personal. She’s observant, defensive, and emotionally armored, but the script keeps exposing the child underneath the badge: the daughter who never got closure, the woman who reads patterns into the sky, and the investigator who can’t stop following the feeling that the world is lying to her.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jodie Foster in The Silence of the Lambs or Amy Adams in Arrival — a hyper-competent investigator whose interior life is the real engine of the movie. It gives an actress the chance to play procedural authority, grief, paranoia, and eventual revelation in one lead role that can carry a prestige genre feature.

lead_characters.name: Dale Cole
lead_characters.hook: Cole is the seasoned field hand who looks like he’s one retirement speech away from disappearing, but he’s still the smartest person in the room when the room gets weird. He’s profane, practical, and unexpectedly tender, with a lived-in loneliness that makes his mentorship of Rico feel earned rather than ornamental.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad’s early seasons or Jeff Bridges in The Old Man — a weathered professional whose humor and weariness are doing the same job at once. It gives a veteran actor a role with authority, comic timing, and a late-career emotional center that can steal scenes without taking the movie away from the lead.

lead_characters.name: Captain Watson
lead_characters.hook: Watson is the polished institutional face of the bureau, all command voice, public confidence, and controlled warmth. He reads as the adult in the room until the script reveals that his calm is the mechanism of the horror, making him a bureaucratic predator who weaponizes procedure as easily as a gun.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Michael Shannon in Boardwalk Empire or Bryan Cranston in Trumbo the chance to weaponize authority and then invert it. It offers a strong character actor the pleasure of playing a man whose public decency and private menace are both fully legible.

lead_characters.name: James White
lead_characters.hook: James is the soft-spoken, emotionally open man who seems like a fellow traveler in Rico’s grief before the story reveals how deeply he’s been folded into the system. He’s vulnerable, sincere, and quietly tragic, which makes him both a romantic possibility and a devastating instrument of the conspiracy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Dano in Prisoners or Jesse Plemons in The Power of the Dog — a gentle presence that can turn unsettling without losing humanity. It gives an actor the chance to play tenderness, dread, and betrayal in the same role, which is catnip for prestige-minded performers.

lead_characters.name: Hope
lead_characters.hook: Hope is the eerie domestic presence who initially reads as a worried wife and gradually becomes the face of the house’s deeper logic. She’s calm, ritualized, and spiritually attuned to the comet, which makes her feel less like a neighbor and more like a gatekeeper to the film’s hidden mythology.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Toni Collette in Hereditary or Rebecca Ferguson in Doctor Sleep a chance to make domestic space feel haunted from the inside. It’s a compact but memorable part for an actress who can make ordinary behavior feel charged with dread.

lead_characters.name: Lear
lead_characters.hook: Lear is the quieter half of the domestic pair, the one who looks like he’s trying to keep the machinery of belief running without letting the seams show. He’s controlled, anxious, and physically committed to the house’s rituals, which makes him feel like a believer who has already paid the price.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Stuhlbarg in A Serious Man or Richard Jenkins in The Shape of Water — a man whose stillness carries dread and sorrow at once. It gives a character actor a chance to play devotion, fear, and complicity without needing big speeches.

lead_characters.name: Isaac Martinez
lead_characters.hook: Isaac is the first body in the chain, but the script gives him enough humanity to feel like more than a victim. He’s wary, funny, and trying to survive his own bad decisions, which makes his fate feel like the first clue that the city’s hidden machinery runs on disposable men.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Benicio del Toro in Traffic or Michael Peña in End of Watch a chance to make a supporting part feel lived-in and dangerous. It’s a compact showcase for an actor who can bring charisma to a man who knows he’s already in too deep.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to turn procedural surveillance into cosmic paranoia.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors with a strong genre short, or established indie directors looking to make a contained commercial swing. The material rewards filmmakers who care about tension through observation, controlled reveals, and performance-forward dread rather than spectacle for its own sake.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a clean visual system: monitors, bugs, windows, foil, and one neighborhood that keeps recontextualizing itself. It also offers a rare chance to stage a horror reveal through procedure and sound design, which is exactly the kind of craft flex directors use to announce a voice.

buyer_appeal.detail: The cast can be built around one strong female lead and a veteran male partner, so it does not require a four-quadrant ensemble to function. The contained neighborhood footprint and high-concept hook make it exportable as a genre title with a clear trailer image and a strong streamer thumbnail.

considerations.area: The red-door/blue-door confusion carries the whole middle.
considerations.detail: The midpoint misdirection is one of the script’s sharpest engines, and the version of the movie where that logic is seeded even earlier would make the eventual reveal feel even more inevitable. A next pass could keep the audience tracking the house geography just a beat sooner so the turn lands with maximum force.

considerations.area: Watson’s cover story is the final lock.
considerations.detail: The institutional reveal is strong, and the script already commits to it in the hospital, the support group, and the dungeon. One direction would be to clarify the exact logic of how Watson’s system works a touch earlier so the final confrontation feels even more devastating rather than merely surprising.

considerations.area: The support-group thread can do more lifting.
considerations.detail: The James material gives Rico a second emotional lane outside the FBI, and it already pays off in the final betrayal. There is room for that relationship to carry a little more independent weight earlier, which would deepen the emotional turn when he becomes part of the machinery.

considerations.area: The production footprint is contained but creature-heavy.
considerations.detail: The story lives in a manageable set of recurring spaces, but the dungeon finale, foil transformations, and comet imagery ask for disciplined effects planning. A simplification lever would be to keep the creature language consistent and economical so the movie preserves its contained-thriller advantage.

The script uses a lot of recognizable institutions and consumer names, from Reynolds Wrap to QuickTime to Bud Light and Cup-o-Noodles. A clearance pass would be straightforward to manage, but it’s worth deciding which names are doing real storytelling work and which can be generalized without changing the feel.
